title: Le héros du jour  (The Hero of the Day)

segments.t: The agency gathers to celebrate Mathias. His colleagues believe he pretended to leave in order to save ASK from the sale. Camille quietly asks her father whether he really intended to go, while Arlette keeps the celebration moving. First, listen in French.
Jean Gabin aussi. Dis pardon, Jean Gabin.
Il est bon, ce pétillant. Un peu vert.
Let's go through the exchange. Arlette even asks her dog Jean Gabin to apologise for his earlier bite.
Jean Gabin aussi. Dis pardon, Jean Gabin.
'Jean Gabin too. Say sorry, Jean Gabin.' Arlette asks her dog to apologise for biting Mathias earlier. The action telling him to say something is a casual command to one listener.
'No problem.' This everyday short response accepts an apology without a whole sentence. The negative word reduces the article before problem.
'Good boy!' The describing word means good or well-behaved here. Arlette is praising her male dog, rather than describing bravery in a dangerous situation.
'A thought for Samuel!' A brief toast can name a thought for someone who is absent. The word for thought is feminine, so it begins with the feminine form of an indefinite article.
'You were never going to leave?' Camille addresses Mathias casually. The past form of going combines with the negative meaning never to ask about his earlier intentions.
'No! Do you doubt it?' The object before doubting refers back to his claim. Mathias answers his daughter's question, then asks whether she believes him.
'A bit. But that's me.' The short expression at the start means a small amount. The independent form of me is used when Camille describes this as part of her character.
'What a killjoy!' This compound describes someone who spoils a cheerful mood. The exclamation begins with a masculine form matching the word for killjoy.
'To ASK!' A toast places the short word meaning to before the person or organisation being celebrated. Mathias names ASK.
'To ASK!' Camille repeats the same toast as the glasses are raised. No full action word is needed when everyone is already joining the celebration.
'Long life!' The description meaning long takes a feminine ending to match life. Together the two words form a wish for a lasting future.
Il est bon, ce pétillant. Un peu vert.

'It's good, this bubbly. A little unripe.' The word for sparkling wine is masculine here. The final description literally means green; for a young wine it can suggest an unripe or sharp taste. Now let's listen to the entire dialogue once more.
Jean Gabin aussi. Dis pardon, Jean Gabin.
Il est bon, ce pétillant. Un peu vert.

That closes episode four. Audrey has a promising new film opportunity, Sofia has her first screen role, and the sale of ASK has fallen through. Mathias stays with colleagues who now see him as their accidental hero. See you next time!
